title: Obesity Phenotypes, Left Atrial Dysfunction, and Cardiovascular Outcomes in HFpEF: A Causal Study Integrating Imaging, Biomarkers, and Genetics in the UK Biobank
notes: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is strongly linked to obesity and remains poorly understood, with limited treatment options. Not all obesity carries the same cardiovascular risk: visceral fat is more harmful than overall body weight, yet most research still relies on BMI alone. This study investigates how different obesity patterns affect the left atrium and whether left atrial dysfunction drives the risk of atrial fibrillation, heart failure hospitalisation, and cardiovascular death in people with HFpEF. Research questions: (1) Which obesity measures, including waist-based indices, body fat percentage, and MRI-derived visceral fat, are most causally linked to left atrial dysfunction and cardiovascular events? (2) How do inflammation, insulin resistance, and metabolic disturbances mediate this relationship? (3) Are there distinct metabolic subtypes of HFpEF that may respond differently to treatment? Using UK Biobank data from approximately 500,000 participants, we will combine cardiac imaging, blood biomarkers, metabolomics, ECG, and genetic data. The study is designed as a target trial emulation - a rigorous causal inference framework that mimics a clinical trial using observational data - with inverse probability weighting to control for confounding. Mendelian randomisation will use genetic variants as natural experiments to strengthen causal conclusions. Mediation analyses will map the biological pathways from obesity to atrial damage. Findings will inform clinical guidelines, support earlier detection of atrial dysfunction, and identify low-cost risk markers applicable in resource-limited healthcare settings.

title: Mechanisms of Neurovascular Unit Failure Driven by "Small VLDL-GlycA": A Multi-Omics and Eye-Brain-Body Axis Study
institution: Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University
notes: Rationale: Accumulating evidence suggests neurodegeneration is a systemic metabolic failure. We propose an "Eye-Brain-Body" axis hypothesis: a specific "pro-inflammatory lipid" phenotype-characterized by Small VLDL particles (high endothelial permeability) and GlycA (chronic inflammation)-acts as a "dual-hit" stressor, causing synchronous Neurovascular Unit (NVU) failure in both the retina and brain. Objectives: 1. Define Metabolic Risk: Utilizing Nightingale NMR data (N~500k), we will isolate the "Small VLDL-GlycA" interaction phenotype and validate its predictive power for dementia using Cox models, moving beyond traditional lipid profiles. 2. Map Eye-Brain Synchronization: We will apply Sparse Canonical Correlation Analysis (sCCA) to the paired Eye-Brain imaging cohort (N~100k). Crucially, to prevent head-motion artifacts from mimicking cortical atrophy, we will implement the "Euler Ladder" topological quality control strategy. We aim to identify structural covariance between retinal layer thinning (OCT) and hippocampal atrophy (MRI). 3. Uncover Molecular Mechanisms: Using UKB-PPP Olink proteomics (N~54k), we will employ High-dimensional Mediation Analysis (HIMA) to identify circulating proteins (e.g., GDF15, NfL) that mediate the pathway from metabolic stress to NVU damage. 4. Establish Causality: We will use Network Mendelian Randomization (Network MR) with Steiger filtering to strictly infer causal directions, controlling for the high pleiotropy of lipid genes. Scientific Value: We aim to validate retinal imaging as a non-invasive "holographic window" for brain health. By integrating metabolomics, proteomics, and imaging, this study will reveal specific targets for early intervention in Alzheimer's disease.

title: Long-term health trajectories following anxiety disorders in UK Biobank
notes: Mental health conditions are increasingly recognised as having long-term implications for physical health and mortality, yet their dynamic relationships with subsequent disease development remain insufficiently understood in real-world populations. This project aims to investigate long-term health trajectories following common mental health conditions, using anxiety disorders as an initial and illustrative exposure. The study will examine how the onset of anxiety disorders is associated with subsequent risks of major physical diseases and all-cause mortality over extended follow-up. The objectives are to: (1) characterise temporal associations between anxiety disorders and incident disease outcomes; (2) examine how these risks evolve over time using time-varying analytical approaches; (3) explore downstream disease pathways leading from mental health conditions to physical morbidity and death. The scientific rationale is that mental health conditions often precede and interact with physical disease processes through behavioural, physiological, and healthcare-related mechanisms. Understanding these trajectories in a large population-based cohort can inform long-term risk assessment and integrated care strategies.

title: Joint Associations of Dietary Intake Patterns and Lifestyle Behaviours with Incident Chronic Disease and Weight Change in UK Biobank
notes: Chronic diseases and excess weight gain remain leading contributors to long-term morbidity and health-care burden worldwide, and many of these outcomes are preventable through modifiable behaviours. Diet and lifestyle habits do not operate in isolation: dietary intake patterns are closely intertwined with behaviours such as physical activity, smoking, alcohol consumption, sleep, and sedentary time, and their combined effects may be larger (or different in direction) than the sum of individual components. However, much of the existing evidence evaluates diet or single lifestyle factors separately, relies on cross-sectional designs, or focuses on single outcomes, which limits causal inference and provides an incomplete basis for integrated prevention strategies. In particular, there is a need for large prospective studies that can (i) characterise real-world dietary patterns and lifestyle behaviour profiles, (ii) quantify their independent and joint associations with incident chronic disease and weight change, and (iii) formally test interaction (synergy/antagonism) and heterogeneity across population subgroups. UK Biobank provides an exceptional platform to address these gaps due to its large sample size, detailed baseline phenotyping, comprehensive dietary and lifestyle assessments, and long-term linkage to health outcomes. By integrating dietary intake patterns with lifestyle behaviours in a unified analytical framework, this project will generate interpretable diet-lifestyle risk profiles, clarify whether combined behavioural patterns confer disproportionate risk or protection, and identify subgroups most likely to benefit from targeted prevention and weight-management strategies. The findings will strengthen the evidence base for integrated, actionable public-health recommendations and more precise behavioural risk stratification.

title: Shared comorbidity signatures and biomarkers in hearing loss and traumatic brain injury: a UK Biobank population data-mining study
notes: This project will use UK Biobank data to investigate shared multimorbidity patterns and biological markers in people with hearing loss and those with traumatic brain injury (TBI), and to assess whether these shared signatures are linked to important downstream health outcomes. Research questions 1. Do individuals with hearing loss and individuals with TBI share a reproducible pattern of co-occurring diseases and risk factors in the general population? 2. Which routinely measured biomarkers (e.g., blood biochemistry and haematology measures; and brain imaging-derived measures in the imaging subset) are associated with both hearing loss and TBI? 3. Do shared comorbidity/biomarker signatures improve prediction of adverse outcomes (e.g., cognitive impairment/dementia, depression, falls) beyond standard demographic and clinical risk factors? Objectives Define hearing loss and TBI using harmonised algorithms based on self-reported information, assessment measures (where available), and linked healthcare records. Quantify and compare comorbidity profiles for hearing loss and TBI, and identify overlapping disease clusters using robust statistical methods with appropriate adjustment for confounding factors and multiple testing. Test associations between shared biomarker profiles and subsequent health outcomes using time-to-event analyses and internally validated prediction models. Produce reproducible outputs (transparent phenotype definitions, code lists, and analysis scripts) to support replication and future research. Scientific rationale Hearing loss and TBI are common, heterogeneous conditions that can lead to long-term neurological, psychiatric, and functional consequences. Both are frequently accompanied by other chronic diseases and may involve overlapping mechanisms such as neuroinflammation, vascular dysfunction, and metabolic dysregulation.

title: Multi-Omics Profiling of Liver Diseases: Integrating Genomics, Metabolomics, Proteomics and Imaging Biomarkers for Hepatology Research
institution: Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital , University of Electronic Science and Technology of China.
notes: Liver diseases including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and hepatocellular carcinoma represent a growing global health burden with complex pathogenesis and progression pathways. The molecular mechanisms underlying liver disease development remain incompletely characterized, particularly regarding the interplay between genetic predisposition, metabolic dysregulation, inflammatory responses, and structural liver damage. This study aims to comprehensively elucidate the multi-omics landscape of liver diseases using UK Biobank's extensive multimodal data. We will first identify genomic variants associated with various liver conditions, focusing on pathways involving lipid metabolism, immune regulation, fibrogenesis, and detoxification processes. Second, we will analyze plasma metabolomic and proteomic profiles to characterize circulating biomarkers that reflect hepatic function, injury severity, and disease activity, including metabolites related to bile acid metabolism, lipid species, and inflammatory mediators. Third, we will integrate quantitative imaging features from abdominal MRI, ultrasound, and elastography with molecular data to develop predictive models for disease progression and complication risks. Our integrated approach will bridge molecular mechanisms with clinical manifestations, ultimately aiming to improve early detection accuracy and enable personalized management strategies for patients with various liver conditions.

title: Mitochondria-wide Association Study (miWAS) for Investigating Roles of Mitochondrial DNA variants in Human diseases
notes: This research aims to investigate the broader implications of mitochondrial DNA variants for a range of diseases and molecular alterations at the level of transcriptomics, epigenomics, and metabolomics. We plan to leverage the vast data resources available from the UK Biobank to analyze the genomic, clinical, and phenotypic data to uncover previously unrecognized links between mitochondrial DNA variant and complex diseases. The project will further inform precision medicine approaches for mitochondrial diseases and provide insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying these conditions. Mitochondria are central to cellular energy production, and dysfunction in mitochondrial genes is implicated in a wide range of diseases, including metabolic disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, and some mental health conditions. To date, more than 350 mitochondrial DNA variants have been reported globally; however, current research on mitochondrial genetics and its role in human health remains limited, and existing studies have primarily focused on either a single disorder or a specific variant. The exploration of mitochondrial-wide genetic variations and their broader implications for human health is still an under-explored area with immense potential for scientific discovery. A Mitochondria-wide Association Study is a hypothesis-free, high-throughput analytical method used to investigate the relationship between mitochondrial genetic variation and complex human diseases or traits. It is conceptually analogous to a Genome-wide Association Study, but with its scope strictly confined to the mitochondrial genome. It serves as the bridge between basic mitochondrial genetics and clinical epidemiology and allows researchers to survey the entire mitochondrial genome in thousands of individuals simultaneously, providing a statistical framework to quantify how the mitochondrial DNA variants influence human health.

title: Blood Pressure Variability and Dementia Risk
notes: Elevated blood pressure variability (BPV) is a risk factor for cerebral small vessel disease, neurodegeneration, and dementia, even when average blood pressure levels are aggressively controlled. Not all individuals with high BPV develop neurodegeneration and dementia, and the susceptibility factors that underly this differential burden are not understood. Additionally, therapeutics that manage BPV or BPV susceptibility factors have not been identified. To address these knowledge gaps we are analyzing potential susceptibility factors to neurodegeneration related to elevated BPV, and therapeutics with the potential to modify BPV or susceptibility to BPV in order to answer the following research questions:1) What is the role of reactive astrogliosis in BPV-induced neurodegenerative pathophysiology, 2) What is the role of cerebrovascular dysfunction in BPV-induced neurodegenerative pathophysiology, 3) What is the role of impaired angiogenic signaling in BPV-induced neurodegenerative pathophysiology, 4) Does strict adherence to an antihypertensive medication regime reduce BPV, 5) Do brain-penetrant antihypertensive medications reduce BPV or the adverse effects of elevated BPV, and 6) Does the presence of at least one copy of the APOE4 allele modify any of these relationships.

title: Validating multi-omics biomarkers for obesity-associated osteoarthritis
notes: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis, affecting over 600 million people worldwide in 2020 and projected to approach 1 billion by 2050. Obesity is the strongest modifiable risk factor for OA, accounting for approximately 20% of the population attributable fraction and, in our data, up to 60% among patients with end-stage disease. With 43% of adults globally overweight and 16% obese, obesity constitutes a growing public health burden. Individuals with both obesity and OA therefore represent a large and clinically challenging subgroup. Recognizing obesity-associated OA as a distinct clinical and biological phenotype is critical to enable targeted prevention, clarify its specific pathophysiology, and advance precision therapeutics. To address this gap, we conducted a preliminary multi-omics study generating evidence that obesity-associated OA is biologically distinct. Integrated metabolomic and proteomic profiling identified PC ae C40:6 as a potential protective metabolite and a panel of ten plasma proteins-including LEP, FABP4, and IGFBP1-that robustly discriminate obesity-associated OA. Exploratory gut microbiome analyses further linked specific microbial taxa to metabolic pathways relevant to this phenotype. However, independent validation is required before clinical translation. Leveraging the UK Biobank, which includes detailed OA phenotyping, genome-wide genotyping, and large-scale proteomics, we propose to validate our proteomic findings and assess causality using a one-sample two-stage Mendelian randomization framework. Specific objectives are: 1. To conduct proteome-wide association analyses of obesity-associated OA, defined as individuals with OA (physician-diagnosed or primary OA-related joint replacement) and BMI !30. 2. To perform Mendelian randomization analyses to evaluate the causal effects of identified proteomic markers on obesity-associated OA risk.

title: Comparative proteogenomics of neurodegenerative disease for precision medicine
notes: We will use UK Biobank's linked genotypes, large-scale plasma proteomics and longitudinal health records to understand how inherited genetic risk for neurodegenerative disease is expressed at the protein level, and how these molecular signatures relate to clinical phenotypes and outcomes. Building on our recent work showing that a major neurodegeneration risk allele is associated with a reproducible, immune-related systemic proteomic signature across multiple disorders, we will extend this comparative proteogenomic framework at population scale across a broader set of established neurodegenerative disease risk alleles. Our research will ask which risk alleles are associated with robust, replicable changes in circulating proteins and pathways, which proteogenomic effects are shared across diseases versus disease-specific, how they vary with clinical and environmental context such as age, sex, cardiometabolic factors and lifestyle, and whether allele-linked protein signatures help stratify clinically relevant outcomes including incident diagnosis, prognosis, multimorbidity, and mortality. The project will map allele-protein associations and implicated pathways using machine learning, compare signatures across neurodegenerative diseases to identify convergent biology and distinct mechanisms, and link these signatures to longitudinal outcomes to prioritise biomarker candidates and therapeutic hypotheses that support precision prevention and treatment.

title: Multi-organ MR imaging for cardiovascular disease phenotype prediction in diabetes: UK Biobank development and hospital validation
institution: Renji Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine
notes: Obesity and diabetes are associated with adverse cardiovascular biomarkers and mortality risk, but current risk models fail to capture systemic multi-organ pathology. We propose developing a novel cardiovascular disease phenotype prediction model for diabetes using multi-organ MR parameters, including native T1 mapping (liver, kidney, pancreas, myocardium) to quantify fibrosis and inflammation, Dixon MRI-derived thigh muscle composition (volume, intramuscular fat) to assess sarcopenia, cardiac function parameters (LVEF, strain), and visceral adipose tissue volumes. Using UK Biobank as development cohort (n!5,000-8,000 diabetic patients with MR, ~43,000+ with organ-specific T1 mapping) and our hospital cohort for external validation, we will: (1) identify independent imaging predictors via Cox proportional hazards regression, penalized LASSO, and machine learning methods (random survival forests, gradient boosting); (2) develop and internally validate a comprehensive risk stratification model with cross-validation and bootstrap techniques; (3) externally validate transportability and assess calibration in real-world clinical settings; (4) evaluate incremental value beyond traditional risk factors using net reclassification improvement and decision curve analysis. This addresses critical gaps in diabetes-specific multi-organ risk assessment, leverages shared MR modalities between UK Biobank and hospital cohorts, and could enable personalized prevention strategies targeting high-risk diabetic patients for intensive cardiovascular risk management.

title: Assessing Environmental Pollutant Impact on Cancer
notes: Research Questions: (1) What are the epidemiological associations between environmental pollutant exposure and the risk of specific cancers and which populations can be identified as highly susceptible groups? (2) What are the pathways, biomarkers, and driving mechanisms underlying carcinogenesis induced by environmental pollutants? (3) Can we develop accurate risk prediction models for environment-related cancers, thereby supporting precision medicine and precision prevention? Objectives: (1) Identify susceptible populations and investigate gene-environment interactions; (2) Explore key risk factors and conduct comprehensive phenotypic analyses; (3) Identify cancer-related biomarkers using proteomics, metabolomics and other omics approaches; (4) Examine the modifying effects of lifestyle factors among genetically susceptible individuals and support evidence-based disease prevention. Accumulating evidence indicates that environmental, genetic and omics factors jointly drive cancer development and progression. However, the independent and synergistic effects of environmental pollutant on cancer, together with the regulatory roles of genetic and omics profiles, remain incompletely understood. UK biobank consists of a large population sample of 500,000 individuals and provides high-quality information on the cancer and environmental pollutant. We aim to explore the associations between environmental pollutant and cancer and establish risk prediction models for cancer.

title: Multi-omics investigation of biological determinants, risk prediction and disease burden of cardiovascular disease in a large prospective cohort
institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences &Peking Union Medical College
notes: This project aims to investigate biological determinants, risk stratification, and disease burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD) using multi-omics data in a large prospective population cohort. Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Although traditional risk factors such as blood pressure, lipids, and lifestyle factors are well established, substantial residual risk remains unexplained. Advances in large-scale biobanks and multi-omics profiling provide an opportunity to examine cardiovascular disease from an integrated biological perspective. We will examine a wide range of biological measures, including hematological indices, biochemical and lipid biomarkers, inflammatory and metabolic markers, genetic variation, polygenic risk scores, and available proteomic data. In a subcohort, cardiovascular imaging-derived phenotypes will be analysed to explore structural and functional correlates of biological risk profiles. The objectives are: (1) to identify biomarkers and biological profiles associated with incident cardiovascular outcomes; (2) to construct composite biological risk indices integrating multi-layer data; (3) to evaluate their prospective associations with major cardiovascular events; (4) to assess incremental predictive value beyond established clinical risk factors; and (5) to explore potential causal relationships using genetic approaches. Population-level disease burden attributable to adverse biological profiles will also be quantified. This integrated framework will improve understanding of cardiovascular disease mechanisms and may enhance risk prediction and prevention strategies.

title: Life-course risk factors for cardiometabolic diseases: influence of early-life risk factors, risk factor trajectories and generations
notes: Cardiovascular risk assessment, such as with the Framingham risk and SCORE2 scores, is largely based on the analyses of cross-sectional measures of cardiovascular risk factors, such as high blood pressure, smoking and high LDL cholesterol levels. Importantly, these measures are often only taken when an individual visits a clinic and when there is a certain indication. However, cardiovascular disease develops over a long period of time as the consequence of cumulative and interacting exposures to these risk factors, which are not stable over time. Furthermore, these risk factor trajectories (e.g., weight trajectory, blood pressure trajectory) are likely to be dependent on early-life exposures, such as birth weight, weight at age 10, number of children. However, this is yet still poorly examined due to the availability of sufficient data and the availability of suitable analytical techniques which our team has been developing over the past years. Within this UK Biobank project, we aim to use the GP assessments to map different risk factor trajectories and aim to link these to incident cardiometabolic diseases later in life. These associations might differ for different generations. We hypothesize that the use of risk factor trajectories will be benefitting clinical care in the end due to improved risk prediction performance as more data is taking into account. Research questions: - Investigate the associations between genomic, generation, early-life (parental) risk factors and risk factor trajectories accross the life course. - Examine the predictive performance of risk factor trajectories on cardiovascular disease, on top of established cardiovascular prediction scores.

title: Discovery of Subclinical Heart-Brain Disease Biomarkers via Self-Supervised and Multimodal Learning
notes: Scientific Rationale: The "Heart-Brain Axis" represents a complex physiological interplay where cardiovascular dysfunction significantly increases the risk of neurodegenerative diseases and stroke. However, traditional statistical methods often fail to capture the high-dimensional, non-linear interactions between cardiac and cerebral systems. UK Biobank provides an unprecedented resource of paired cardiac and brain MRI, genetics, and longitudinal clinical outcomes. We propose to apply state-of-the-art artificial intelligence and deep learning techniques to this multimodal dataset to uncover novel biomarkers and mechanistic pathways linking heart and brain health. Research Questions: 1. Can deep learning algorithms extract novel, subclinical imaging phenotypes from cardiac and brain MRI that are superior to conventional metrics in predicting comorbidity risk? 2. How do high-dimensional genetic and metabolic profiles interact with imaging markers to drive the progression of heart-brain comorbidities? 3. Can multimodal deep learning models improve the early prediction of dementia and stroke in patients with cardiovascular disease compared to standard clinical risk scores? Objectives: We will develop an end-to-end multimodal AI framework for the heart-brain axis by (i) building and validating computer-vision pipelines for automated segmentation and feature extraction from cardiac and brain MRI, (ii) constructing integrative deep learning models that fuse imaging with genomics and electronic health records to uncover shared, non-linear risk factors linking cardiovascular and neurological conditions, and (iii) applying unsupervised, data-driven clustering to identify distinct patient subgroups with characteristic patterns of heart-brain dysfunction, enabling more precise risk stratification and targeted prevention.

title: Assessing the impact of cardiometabolic risk factors on prognosis in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease and establish a prediction model
notes: Background & Rationale Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease has been redefined as Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD), highlighting the central role of cardiometabolic risk factors (CMRFs) like obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and insulin resistance. While individual CMRFs are linked to poorer outcomes in MASLD, their combined and interactive effects on disease progression, mortality, and liver-related events are not well quantified. Furthermore, clinically useful models integrating multiple CMRFs and genetic data to stratify patient prognosis are lacking. Research Questions & Objectives This project aims to leverage the rich phenotypic, genetic, and metabolic data in the UK Biobank to: Systematically evaluate the joint effects of CMRFs on liver fibrosis and long-term clinical outcomes (all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, chronic kidney disease, liver-related events) in individuals with MASLD. Identify genetic and metabolic markers that modify the association between CMRFs and MASLD progression. Develop and validate an integrated, clinically actionable risk-stratification model that combines clinical, metabolic, and genetic data to distinguish between low- and high-risk MASLD patients. Scientific Rationale By clarifying the synergistic impact of CMRFs, this research will identify high-risk subgroups and potential metabolic pathways for intervention. The expected outcome is a validated risk-stratification tool to guide monitoring and therapeutic strategies for MASLD patients in clinical care, with implications for public health policy and screening programs focused on multi-morbid metabolic dysfunction.

title: Identification of Novel Therapeutic Targets for Aortic Diseases and Atherosclerosis using UK Biobank Genomic Data.
institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
notes: Research Questions: How do genetic, metabolic, and environmental determinants interact to drive the pathogenesis, progression, and clinical outcomes of complex cardiovascular diseases, with a specific focus on aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, and atherosclerosis? What are the underlying systemic molecular networks that can serve as novel targets for early diagnosis and therapeutic intervention? Objectives: 1) To systematically identify novel genetic architectures, including rare variants and gene-environment interactions, associated with the susceptibility and progression of aortic and atherosclerotic diseases. 2) To leverage the extensive genomic, metabolomic, and proteomic datasets within the UK Biobank to construct multi-omics integration models, elucidating systemic metabolic reprogramming and cross-tissue communication mechanisms. 3) To discover and clinically validate novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets, facilitating drug repurposing screening and precision medicine strategies for cardiovascular risk stratification and management. title: Comprehensive profiling of genetic, multi-omics, imaging, and lifestyle determinants for the trajectory and prognosis of coronary artery disease
institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences &Peking Union Medical College
notes: Research Questions: 1) How do complex interactions among genetic susceptibility, anthropometric profiles (including imaging-derived body composition and muscle mass), and multidimensional lifestyle factors drive the onset and progression of coronary artery disease (CAD)? 2) Can we construct a robust, multi-modal risk prediction model for the full trajectory of CAD and its adverse outcomes? Objectives: This project constitutes the core of my doctoral dissertation. The primary objectives are: 1) To systematically evaluate the joint effects of polygenic/monogenic traits (using WES/WGS data) and comprehensive lifestyle factors on CAD incidence. 2) To exploit imaging data (e.g., cardiac MRI, abdominal MRI) to explore the prognostic value of body composition (such as fat distribution and skeletal muscle mass/sarcopenia indices) in CAD patients. 3) To develop and validate an integrated predictive model combining clinical, genetic, and imaging parameters to stratify cardiovascular risk, guiding early intervention. Scientific Rationale: While traditional risk factors are well-established, a considerable proportion of cardiovascular events still occur in individuals with varying risk profiles, highlighting the limitations of current assessment strategies. Previous investigations often focused on isolated dimensions, such as individual lifestyle components or basic standard modifiable cardiovascular risk factors (SMuRFs). However, CAD is a systemic metabolic syndrome. By leveraging the full UK Biobank cohort, this doctoral project will integrate multi-dimensional data-spanning whole-genome sequencing, extensive biochemical assays, physical measurements, linked health records, and sophisticated imaging data -to decode the hidden pathways of cardiovascular disease. This holistic approach will not only map the longitudinal trajectory of CAD but also identify novel therapeutic targets and subgroups, fundamentally supporting the completion of my doctoral thesis.

title: Sarcopenia Trajectories and Cardiovascular Multimorbidity: Investigating the Mediating Role of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis in the UK Biobank
notes: Sarcopenia, characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of cardiometabolic health. Previous studies have reported associations between sarcopenia and cardiovascular disease, but most rely on single baseline measurements and do not capture the dynamic progression of muscle decline. Longitudinal trajectories of sarcopenia may better reflect cumulative metabolic deterioration and long-term cardiovascular risk. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is strongly linked with insulin resistance, systemic inflammation, and cardiovascular disease. Skeletal muscle and liver are metabolically interconnected organs, suggesting a potential muscle-liver-cardiovascular pathway. However, whether MASH mediates the relationship between sarcopenia progression and cardiovascular multimorbidity has not been systematically investigated in large population-based cohorts. This study aims to examine whether distinct trajectories of sarcopenia are associated with different risks of developing cardiovascular multimorbidity and to evaluate whether MASH mediates this relationship. Using the UK Biobank cohort, sarcopenia-related indicators will be derived from measurements such as appendicular lean mass and handgrip strength. Trajectories of sarcopenia will be identified using trajectory modelling approaches. Cardiovascular multimorbidity will be defined as the coexistence of two or more cardiovascular diseases and will be identified through linkage with hospital inpatient records, primary care data, and death registry data. Associations will be evaluated using time-to-event analyses with adjustment for potential confounders. Mediation analyses will be performed to assess the potential role of MASH. This project is conducted for academic research purposes under appropriate academic supervision, with the student taking primary responsibility for the research.

title: Trajectory-Based Multimodal Risk Assessment of Type 2 Diabetes and Associated Cardiovascular and Neurological Outcomes
notes: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a complex metabolic disorder associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and neurological complications, including stroke and dementia. These complications share common underlying mechanisms, including insulin resistance and accelerated atherosclerosis. However, the specific pathways linking T2D to these outcomes are not fully understood. Furthermore, differences in genetic, lifestyle, and longitudinal factors between cross-ethnic populations, such as European (i.e., UK Biobank) and South Asian (i.e., Indian) populations, may influence disease trajectories and complication risks. This study aims to implement an AI-driven, trajectory-based, multimodal framework using data from the UK Biobank (UKB). Multimodal data will include imaging biomarkers (e.g., carotid ultrasound), electronic health records (EHR), polygenic risk scores (PGS), metabolic markers, and other clinical and lifestyle factors. The proposed framework comprises two stages: 1. Prediction of T2D and generation of a T2D risk score. 2. Assessment of the T2D risk score, along with other covariates, as predictors of CVD and neurological outcomes (e.g., stroke and dementia). To ensure generalizability, the developed multimodal sequential prediction framework will be validated in an independent cohort with comparable data, enabling assessment of cross-ethnic differences in sequential risk profiles. As T2D and Stroke are among the top 10 causes of death in India (reported by WHO), and recent studies have reported an increasing prevalence of dementia in India, plans are underway to initiate collaboration with an Indian or other independent cohort for future validation.

title: Does continuous accelerometer data encode metabolic and cardiovascular health? Representation learning from wearable time-series to predict blood biomarker status
notes: Blood biomarkers like HbA1c, cholesterol, and triglycerides are central to identifying risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, yet blood tests are infrequent and provide only snapshots. Wearable devices, by contrast, capture continuous behavioural data including physical activity patterns, sleep-wake cycles, and sedentary behaviour. Whether this data encodes information about metabolic and cardiovascular health is an open question with significant implications for preventive care. Heydari et al. (2024) showed that self-reported lifestyle factors improve blood biomarker prediction using UK Biobank questionnaire data, and noted the lack of large cohorts with continuous lifestyle measurements as a key limitation. UK Biobank's accelerometer subset, where approximately 100,000 participants wore wrist-worn devices for seven days, offers an opportunity to test whether objectively measured activity data improves on self-report for the same purpose. Our objectives are: (1) test whether features learned from accelerometer time-series contain information about metabolic and cardiovascular biomarkers beyond what age, sex, BMI, and self-reported activity provide; (2) evaluate whether temporal activity patterns add predictive value over simple summary statistics like average acceleration; (3) explore whether learned representations can differentiate individuals with early metabolic dysfunction from those with healthier biomarker profiles. Our approach uses representation learning methods (deep metric learning, temporal embeddings) to extract features from accelerometer data, with biomarker prediction via gradient-boosted and neural models, benchmarked against Heydari et al.'s self-reported lifestyle baseline. This project is led by Project 120 Ltd (trading as Noyu), a health technology company building personalised health models from biomarker and wearable data, with analytical support through Imperial College London's Individual Research Project programme.

title: Evaluation of biomarkers and risk factors for early prediction of cancer
notes: Research question Cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, claiming nearly 10 million lives each year. Due to its extremely complex pathogenesis, there is still a lack of clear and universally applicable preventive measures. Objective To address this research gap, this study aims to employ an integrated analytical strategy, comprehensively utilizing epidemiological data and multi-omics data (including genomics, metabolomics, and proteomics) through multi-dimensional analyses. The objective is to identify novel risk factors, screen potential biomarkers, and elucidate their associations, causal effects, and risk prediction relationships with cancer. Scientific rationale Although traditional observational studies have revealed many cancer risk factors, their findings are often constrained by confounding bias and reverse causation, limiting our ability to map the complete etiological pathway. To bridge this gap, this study will integrate multi-omics (proteomics and metabolomics) with epidemiological data. Using a multi-dimensional analytical strategy, we aim to identify novel risk factors and biomarkers and provide robust causal evidence for cancer associations. This investigation will systematically explore the causal networks underlying major malignancies, including esophageal, lung, liver, and gastric cancers. This project will be undertaken by Yang Tingting as part of her doctoral research, under the supervision of Principal Investigator Wang Jianbo.

title: Elucidating the Renal Axis in Systemic Metabolic Disorders: Integrated Multi-Omics and Clinical Trajectory Modeling of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome
notes: This research aims to elucidate the etiology and prognostic trajectories of kidney diseases within the Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome and systemic metabolic disorders (SMD). Recognizing the kidneys as a critical nexus in cardiovascular, metabolic, and immunological crosstalk, the study maps the longitudinal progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) alongside heart failure and diabetes. By integrating prospective cohort data with multidimensional clinical phenotypes, we will delineate how renal decline intersects with systemic metabolic dysfunction to drive adverse outcomes. To uncover underlying mechanisms, we will employ a multi-omics framework-integrating genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic signatures-to identify molecular drivers of renal impairment. A core component involves using Mendelian randomization and polygenic risk scores to establish causal pathways linking metabolic exposures directly to renal endpoints. Furthermore, we will synthesize electronic health records with radiomic features from renal imaging to identify novel phenotypic subtypes and cryptic pathological pathways defining kidney-related systemic disorders. Ultimately, this initiative leverages AI and sophisticated statistical modeling to engineer high-fidelity risk stratification tools for early detection of renal decline. By evaluating the modulatory effects of lifestyle and social determinants, the project aims to optimize preventative clinical decision-making. These insights will foster precision medicine by enhancing mechanistic understanding of the renal-cardio-metabolic axis and facilitating targeted renoprotective strategies to reduce the global burden of multi-organ metabolic diseases.

title: Multi-Omics and Clinical Integration for Chronic Disease Risk Factor Identification and Predictive Modeling
institution: Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine.
notes: The pathophysiological processes of chronic diseases, such as diabetes and hypertension, are highly complex and characterized by significant dynamic fluctuations. However, traditional clinical monitoring is often constrained to "snapshot" invasive procedures-such as fingerstick blood sampling or arterial catheterization-which carry high infection risks and suffer from low patient compliance. Leveraging the extensive cohort and multidimensional data of the UK Biobank, this study aims to investigate the associations between alternative physiological indicators and chronic diseases to determine their potential as independent predictors. To achieve this, the study will: 1!Apply causal inference methods to identify factors with causal relationships to chronic disease risk from routinely collected physiological parameters; 2!Analyze longitudinal dynamic features to address the limitations of traditional "snapshot" monitoring in capturing hemodynamic instability; 3!Develop precision risk prediction models that integrate multi-omics and longitudinal clinical data. By utilizing the UK Biobank to reveal the dynamic evolutionary mechanisms of chronic diseases, this research seeks to overcome the constraints of traditional invasive monitoring. The development of non-invasive prediction models will significantly alleviate the monitoring burden while providing core technical support for personalized precision prevention.

title: Precision Medicine Research for Musculoskeletal Health: A Population Cohort-Based Study with Multi-Omic Strategies and Deep Phenotyping
notes: This project leverages multi-omic strategies and deep phenotyping to elucidate the pathogenesis and regulatory networks of musculoskeletal health-related disorders, identify biomarkers for precise prevention and diagnosis, and advance population musculoskeletal health management. Musculoskeletal disorders (sarcopenia, sports injuries, degenerative lesions and their comorbidities) are major global public health burdens, causing disability and reduced quality of life. Despite existing research, their onset risk factors, immunometabolic mechanisms, comorbidity patterns, and valid diagnostic/prognostic biomarkers lack systematic population-level validation from large-scale cohort studies. Using UK Biobank's comprehensive dataset-including genomic, biochemical/metabolomic, imaging, clinical phenotype, lifestyle (exercise behavior), comorbidity and disease outcome data-this study explores the biological mechanisms underlying musculoskeletal health, exercise-promoted health effects, muscle aging, sports injuries and their comorbidities. Integrating multi-layer biological and population cohort data, we will dissect the risk factor profiles and comorbidity networks of these disorders, mine immunometabolism-related molecular pathways, and discover specific biomarkers for predicting disease susceptibility, progression and intervention response. Study findings will inform personalized public health interventions (e.g., targeted exercise recommendations) and precision clinical strategies (e.g., biomarker-based early screening and prognostic assessment), ultimately improving population musculoskeletal health and reducing the disease burden on individuals and society.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis and machine learning to dissect shared and disease-specific mechanisms across neurological disorders
notes: Neurological disorders are a major contributor to disability and loss of independence worldwide. Although these conditions are often studied individually, many neurological diseases share overlapping biological pathways, while also displaying disease-specific molecular features. Understanding both the shared and distinct mechanisms across neurological disorders may provide important insights into disease etiology, early detection, and potential therapeutic targets. The UK Biobank provides an unprecedented resource for investigating these questions at population scale, with extensive phenotypic information linked to genetic and multi-omics data, including GWAS, plasma proteomics and metabolomics. The primary research questions are: (1) what molecular features are common across major neurological disorders, and (2) which molecular signatures distinguish specific diseases. To address these questions, we will integrate clinical phenotypes with multi-omics data from the UK Biobank to systematically characterize cross-disease molecular patterns. We will further explore the biological pathways associated with these signatures and assess their potential relevance for disease stratification and risk prediction. By identifying shared and disease-specific molecular features across neurological disorders, this project aims to improve our understanding of the biological architecture underlying these conditions and contribute to the development of more precise approaches for early detection and prevention.

title: Multi-Omics, Imaging and Clinical data Integration to Investigate the Determinants of Complex Musculoskeletal traits and their role in related diseases
notes: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSD) arise from complex interactions between ageing, genetics, environment and metabolism. Large resources like UK Biobank & its multimodal dataset-including longitudinal health records, imaging-derived phenotypes, genomics, proteomics and detailed metabolite and clinical measurements, enables high-resolution investigation of these traits. The transition from physiological aging-related decline to early pathology is poorly understood. Distinguishing these states requires integrating longitudinal phenotypes (e.g., bone mineral density, muscle composition) with imaging-derived structural traits and clinical measurements. Advances in machine learning (ML) and multi-omics now allow for the identification of latent disease subtypes and molecular pathways driving musculoskeletal deterioration and related systemic conditions, which may help us reveal early molecular determinants, disease endo-phenotypes, and biological pathways driving musculoskeletal deterioration and related systemic conditions. Research Questions 1. Do multi-omics profiles improve disease risk prediction compared to traditional clinical risk factors and how to integrate imaging, clinical and omics (genomics, proteomics, metabolomics) to understand disease progression? 2. How do longitudinal musculoskeletal traits change with ageing versus early pathological decline? 3. Can multimodal health data integration identify early indicators of MSD onset or predict disease risk? Objectives 1. Characterise trajectories of musculoskeletal traits using longitudinal and imaging data to distinguish age-related changes (e.g. physical measure, accelerometry, BMD, muscle composition) from early pathological decline that may signal disease initiation independent of chronological ageing. 2. Harmonise EHR, imaging, and omics data to capture comprehensive disease phenotypes. 3. Apply ML-based multiomics integration to identify disease biomarkers & progression patterns
